result.question: Indo-Islamic architecture was a synthesis of indigenous and imported traditions. Elaborate with reference to its structural techniques, decorative forms and major monuments. (Answer in 250 words)

sentences.text: Large-scale Indo-Islamic building began under the Delhi Sultanate in the early thirteenth century, when Turkish rulers combined West Asian forms with Indian materials and craftsmanship.
Its forms drew on Persian, Turkish and Saracenic influences but remained rooted in Indian sensibilities.

Indian builders had relied on trabeation, using pillars, brackets and lintels, but the arcuate method introduced true arches of voussoirs and keystones, and domes on squinches and pendentives that freed interiors of pillars.
As religious art avoided living forms, surfaces were adorned with calligraphy, arabesque and geometric patterns in plaster and stone.
Indian motifs persisted, such as the lotus bud fringe on arches, the inverted lotus atop domes and, in Gujarat, bell and chain carvings borrowed from temples.
Thick rubble walls were cased with chunam plaster or dressed stone, while pietra dura, glazed tiles and jali screens enriched surfaces.
The thirteenth-century Qutub Minar, a tapering tower of red and buff sandstone, came to be associated with the Sufi saint Nizamuddin Auliya.
The fifteenth-century Chand Minar at Golconda, whose facade once bore encaustic tile work, was built by local architects with others from Delhi and Iran.
Provincial styles flourished in Mandu, Gujarat, Bengal and Jaunpur, and a distinct Deccani style developed at Bijapur and Golconda.
Mughal tombs such as Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal were set within charbagh gardens symbolising paradise, while also proclaiming imperial grandeur.
This fusion of arch and lintel, dome and lotus, created a shared architectural heritage whose conservation and study deserve greater public support.
